title: Barometer from the Golden Rule
field_description_long: In 1958, the Golden Rule sailed towards the Marshall Islands to protest nuclear weapons testing. It was the first boat that attempted to disrupt a nuclear test, and this action created publicity and further protests against nuclear testing in the pacific. This barometer from the voyage comes from the Albert Bigelow Papers (DG 076). Bigelow was the captain of the Golden Rule.
image_alt_text: A metal barometer with a glass face. Around the face are numbers to indicate the air pressure; Small lettering in the middle and bottom of the face reads "Selsi", "Holosteric Barometer" , "Copyright 1940 Selsi Co. Inc." and Made in France."

title: Jane Addams' Nobel Peace Prize
field_description_long: The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Jane Addams in 1931 for her lifelong dedication to international relations and disarmament. She was the first American woman to receive the honor.
image_alt_text: Gold medal with Alfred Nobel's profile on one side; On the other side are three naked men embracing, they are surrounded by the words "Pro pace et fraternitate gentium" (For peace and fraternity among peoples).

title: Exchange of Friendly Addresses between women of Exeter and Philadelphia
field_description_long: Friendly Addresses were inspired by Joseph Crosfield, an English Quaker, and Elihu Burritt, an American, to promote friendship between the United States and Great Britain on a person-to-person level. This exchange of two letters between the women of Exeter in England and Philadelphia in the United States  was prompted due to tensions between England and the United States known as the "Oregon Question," a boundary dispute resulting from competing claims to the Pacific Northwest territory.  In this display, the address from Exeter appears first, the reply from Philadelphia appears second, and then all of the signatures on the address from Exeter appear at the end. Click through to each letter to find its transcription.
field_use_reproduction: Please cite appropriately, crediting the item in the Universal Peace Union Records (DG 038), Swarthmore College Peace Collection.

title: To the Women of the City of Philadelphia, and of the United States Generally, the Friendly Address of the Undersigned Women Inhabitants of the City of Exeter in England
field_description_long: Handwritten address; a plea, dated 28th of April 1846, signed by 1623 English women, invoking a common ancestry and urging their American sisters to unite with them "in using the influence we possess, which is not powerless though exerted chiefly around the domestic hearth."

title: From the Women of Philadelphia U.S.A. in Answer to the Friendly Address of the Women of Exeter, England, on the Subject of Peace Resource
field_description_long: Handwritten draft of a reply to an address from women of Exeter, England, in response to their plea urging their American sisters to help prevent war between England and the United States. This draft, of which the final version no longer exists, warns that a mother could sow the seed of blood-thirsty ambition in her son "when in his childish hours she gave him tiny weapons, and taught him how to mimic war's murderous game." It is signed by Lucretia Mott. The reply, which was sent to England and is now lost, was signed by 3,525 Philadelphia women.
